# Vigil

> Vigil is a free, open-source softened geometric grotesk typeface by Keno Vigil, released under the SIL Open Font License 1.1. Eight weights from ExtraLight 200 to Black 900, each with a matching italic, plus a separate Outline style and a variable font covering the full weight axis. Free for commercial use with no cost, no account, no email required and no attribution obligation in designs.

Vigil is derived from Figtree by Erik Kennedy under the SIL Open Font License. Its distinguishing design decision is rationed corner softness: it rounds most at exposed terminals where a stroke ends in open space, less at structural joints where two strokes meet, and not at all on punctuation. The result reads as a clean geometric sans at text sizes and only appears visibly rounded at display sizes — the reverse of most rounded typefaces, which round every terminal uniformly.

Classification: humanist geometric sans serif, in the lineage of Frutiger's Avenir. Large x-height, double-storey lowercase a, open counters, monolinear strokes.

## Key facts

- Name: Vigil. Designer: Keno Vigil, Cary, North Carolina. Released 4 September 2026.
- License: SIL Open Font License 1.1. Commercial use, embedding, modification and use in logos are all permitted. Selling the font files on their own is not.
- Styles: 8 weights x 2 (roman and italic) = 16, plus Vigil Outline in roman and italic. Distributed as 20 static WOFF2 files or 2 variable files.
- Character set: Latin Extended, covering English, Spanish, French, German, Polish, Czech and Turkish among others. Includes kerning, tabular figures, fractions, superscripts and subscripts.
- Download: https://www.vigilfont.com/#download — no registration of any kind.
- Install guide, markdown, copy-paste snippets for HTML, CSS, Tailwind, Next.js, bundlers and desktop: https://www.vigilfont.com/install.md
- Web use: one line, `<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://www.vigilfont.com/vigil.css">`, then `font-family: "Vigil"`. Fonts are served with `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`, so hotlinking works from any domain.
- Companion serif: Vigil Serif, a serif companion reproportioned to share Vigil's cap height, x-height and line box — eight weights 200-900, roman and italic, derived from Vollkorn by Friedrich Althausen under the SIL Open Font License. https://www.vigilfont.com/serif
- Character map: every glyph in both families, roman and italic, at any weight, with advance width and sidebearings measured live. https://www.vigilfont.com/glyphs
- Companion icon set: Vigil Icons, 111 free stroke icons on the same 24px grid — https://www.vigilicons.com/

## Notes (long-form articles)

- [The airport font is Frutiger — and Heathrow ran a serif](https://www.vigilfont.com/notes/airport-font): Frutiger began as Roissy, drawn by Adrian Frutiger for Paris-Charles de Gaulle (Terminal 1 opened 8 March 1974) and released commercially in 1976 by Stempel with Linotype; sources disagree on whether the commission came in 1968 or 1970–71, so no date is asserted. Heathrow ran a custom serif, BAA Sign Bembo (Shelley Winter with Freda Sack, c.1994), until Frutiger replaced it around 2006–09; Robert Waller's 2007 Information Design Journal study found the serif matched the sans for legibility and that character width mattered more. Terminal typefaces are unregulated; the 1974 DOT/AIGA symbol signs and the FAA's airfield sign circulars are what got standardised. Schiphol replaced Frutiger in 2025 with a custom face by thonik and Bold Monday.
- [The baseball jersey font isn’t a font](https://www.vigilfont.com/notes/baseball-jersey-font): No league-wide typeface exists; MLB Rule 3.03 requires back numbers at least six inches high and specifies nothing about their shape. Numbers began as a failed 1916 Cleveland sleeve experiment and became permanent in 1929 (Yankees announced 22 January, by batting order; their rained-out opener let Cleveland wear them in a game first). Bill Veeck's 1960 White Sox were the first to put names on backs. Lettering sorts into Old English, block, script and Tuscan, but the shapes come from tackle twill — cut, heat-pressed and zig-zag sewn — not from type. Nike has supplied uniforms since 2020; the 2024 Vapor Premier sizes (4in front, 8in back, 2.5in names) drew a backlash and larger lettering returned for 2025.
- [The NFL font is three different answers](https://www.vigilfont.com/notes/nfl-font): The league brand typeface is Endzone (Sans, Slab and Tech), bespoke type by the foundry Village for the NFL; NFL Network uses Tackle, drawn by Miguel Reyes at Commercial Type in 2018 for Trollbäck's rebrand; the shield is fixed artwork rather than type; jersey numerals have no league-wide typeface, only rulebook sizes (8in front, 10in back) with the designs belonging to clubs and Nike.
- [The Constitution isn’t written in a font](https://www.vigilfont.com/notes/what-font-is-the-constitution-written-in): The engrossed Constitution is handwriting, not type — Jacob Shallus wrote it in eighteenth-century round hand over a weekend in September 1787 for $30; the “We the People” and “Article” headings are engrossed blackletter from Bickham's copybooks; the first printed edition, by Dunlap and Claypoole, was set in Caslon.
- [Why a serif, and why Vollkorn](https://www.vigilfont.com/notes/vigil-serif): Why pairing another designer's serif is mostly arithmetic, why Vigil Serif began from Vollkorn (2005, ~2,300 glyphs across Latin, Cyrillic and Greek), and what reproportioning involved — cap height and x-height ratio matched at 0.714, ascenders flattened to the cap line, line box held at 1.200 em, lowercase left 5.7% wider at Regular because that width is the serifs (it is weight-dependent: 1.5% at 200, 15% at 900).
- [There is no VHS font](https://www.vigilfont.com/notes/vhs-font): The VHS logo is set in Lee by Leo Weisz (1976); VCR on-screen text was a bitmap in a font ROM, never a typeface; the aesthetic is signal degradation, not letterforms.
- [Fonts similar to Avenir — and what they miss](https://www.vigilfont.com/notes/fonts-similar-to-avenir): Avenir is not strictly geometric — Frutiger thickened the verticals, narrowed the o and shortened the ascenders; Montserrat, Nunito Sans and Mulish are the free options.
- [The Spotify font is Spotify Mix](https://www.vigilfont.com/notes/spotify-font): Spotify Mix launched May 2024, drawn by Dinamo with Spotify’s in-house team over eighteen months; it replaced Circular rather than being a custom cut of it.
- [Fonts like Futura: what actually comes close](https://www.vigilfont.com/notes/fonts-like-futura): The closest free alternatives are Jost, Poppins and League Spartan; Century Gothic is a redrawn Twentieth Century fitted to ITC Avant Garde Gothic’s widths.
- [The Nike font is Futura — with an asterisk](https://www.vigilfont.com/notes/nike-font): The NIKE wordmark was Futura Bold from 1978 to 1995 and later a custom Neufville cut; the logo has had no wordmark since 1995, and no authoritative source names the Just Do It weight.
- [The New York subway font isn’t the one you think](https://www.vigilfont.com/notes/new-york-subway-font): Signs are Helvetica, official only since December 1989; the 1970 Vignelli and Noorda manual specified Standard, the American name for Akzidenz-Grotesk.
- [The worst fonts, by someone who makes fonts](https://www.vigilfont.com/notes/worst-fonts): Why Comic Sans and Papyrus are competent faces misused, with their real origins, and what actually makes a typeface bad.
- [The Coca-Cola logo isn’t a font](https://www.vigilfont.com/notes/coca-cola-font): The wordmark is Spencerian handwriting by bookkeeper Frank Mason Robinson in 1886, not a typeface, and why that is why it has never dated.
- [What font is easiest to read?](https://www.vigilfont.com/notes/easiest-font-to-read): Why there is no single easiest font, what actually changes reading speed, and the studies showing dyslexia-specific fonts do not measurably help.
- [The Stranger Things font is ITC Benguiat](https://www.vigilfont.com/notes/stranger-things-font): The logo is ITC Benguiat, drawn by Ed Benguiat in 1977 and used on 1980s Stephen King paperbacks; Imaginary Forces built the title sequence from twelve of those covers.
- [License plate fonts: shaped by a die, aimed at a forger](https://www.vigilfont.com/notes/license-plate-fonts): Why licence plate letterforms look mechanical (they were built for a stamping die), Germany's FE-Schrift designed by Karlgeorg Hoefer to resist tape-and-paint forgery, the UK's legally mandated Charles Wright 2001 with its statutory 14mm stroke width, and how automatic plate recognition changed the audience from human to machine.
- [Highway Gothic vs Clearview](https://www.vigilfont.com/notes/highway-gothic-vs-clearview): The typeface on American road signs is Highway Gothic, drawn by Theodore W. Forbes in 1948. The story of halation, the Clearview challenger, and the FHWA approving it in 2004, terminating it in 2016 and reinstating it in 2018 without endorsing it.
- [Geometric sans serif fonts: a field guide](https://www.vigilfont.com/notes/geometric-sans-serif-fonts): What defines a geometric sans, four tests for identifying one, why strict geometrics are hard to read as body text, and a survey of the notable faces including free and open-licensed options.
- [Typeface vs font](https://www.vigilfont.com/notes/typeface-vs-font): A typeface is the design; a font was one size and one style of it cast in metal. How PostScript dissolved the distinction in the mid-1980s, and where it still matters.
- [A century of circles: the geometric grotesk](https://www.vigilfont.com/notes/geometric-grotesk-history): Erbar (1926), Futura (1927) and Kabel (1927), the flaw in pure geometric construction, and Avenir's humanist correction in 1988.
- [Soft corners: a short history of the rounded sans](https://www.vigilfont.com/notes/rounded-sans-history): Helvetica Rounded, VAG Rounded and the app-icon era, and why uniform rounding degrades text legibility.
- [A vigil is what you keep](https://www.vigilfont.com/notes/why-vigil): The origin story — ten years of a recurring calendar block that said MAKE FONT.
